prompt: What is the most reliable immediate indicator that bag-valve-mask ventilations are effective?

options.text: Visible chest rise with each ventilation
A pulse oximeter reading that rises within seconds
Resistance felt in the bag as each breath is squeezed
Abdomen rising and falling with each ventilation

explanation: Adequate BVM produces chest rise and improved oxygenation indicators; speaking during BVM means the seal/technique is wrong.

distractorExplanations.b: SpO2 lags behind ventilation by a minute or more and can mislead with poor perfusion or CO; chest rise is the immediate sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising bag resistance suggests airway obstruction, gastric distension, or poor lung compliance, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach (gastric insufflation) from excess volume or poor head position.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1).

prompt: An adult patient with suspected opioid overdose is unresponsive with slow, shallow respirations. After scene safety and airway opening, the priority intervention is

options.text: Place in the recovery position and observe breathing closely
Support ventilation with BVM/oxygen and consider naloxone
Give naloxone and wait for breathing to improve on its own
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and monitor

explanation: Respiratory depression drives opioid morbidity; ventilate and reverse per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position protects the airway but does not fix slow, shallow breathing; ventilations must be assisted.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone takes minutes to act; inadequate ventilation is supported with a BVM first rather than waiting.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather requires adequate spontaneous breathing; slow, shallow respirations need assisted BVM ventilation.

prompt: Which oxygen delivery device typically provides the highest FiO2 for a spontaneously breathing patient when used correctly?

options.text: Nasal cannula at 1 L/min
Simple face mask at 2 L/min
Nonrebreather mask at adequate flow
Room air

explanation: A properly flushed nonrebreather at high flow delivers high FiO2 versus low-flow nasal cannula.

distractorExplanations.a: 1 L NC provides low FiO2.
distractorExplanations.b: 2 L is inadequate for a simple mask and still lower than NRB.
distractorExplanations.d: Room air is ~21% oxygen.

prompt: Stridor in an upper-airway obstruction patient suggests

options.text: Bronchoconstriction of the lower airways
Fluid in the alveoli from acute pulmonary edema
Complete obstruction with no air movement
Partial obstruction at or above the larynx

explanation: Stridor is a hallmark of upper airway narrowing and is an emergency warning sign. It produces a high-pitched inspiratory sound.

distractorExplanations.a: Lower-airway narrowing produces expiratory wheezing, not the inspiratory stridor of an upper airway obstruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales), not the high-pitched inspiratory sound of stridor.
distractorExplanations.c: Complete obstruction is silent; stridor requires air moving past a partial narrowing.

prompt: When suctioning an adult airway, a key safety limit is:

options.text: Limit suction attempts to about 15 seconds
Suction while inserting the catheter to clear more fluid
Insert the rigid tip past the base of the tongue
Limit suction attempts to about 30 seconds in adults

explanation: Prolonged suction causes hypoxia; clear the airway in brief attempts. Preoxygenate as able before and between attempts.

distractorExplanations.b: Suction is applied only while withdrawing the catheter; suctioning on insertion worsens hypoxia and mucosal trauma.
distractorExplanations.c: A rigid catheter is inserted only as far as you can see; passing the base of the tongue triggers gagging and a vagal response.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty seconds is twice the adult limit; prolonged suction causes hypoxia and bradycardia.

prompt: The head-tilt/chin-lift is generally avoided in trauma patients because

options.text: It pushes the tongue back into the airway
It may worsen cervical spine injury
It raises intracranial pressure in head injuries
It is less effective than the jaw-thrust

explanation: Suspected c-spine injury warrants jaw-thrust with spinal motion restriction considerations.

distractorExplanations.a: The maneuver lifts the tongue off the pharynx; the trauma concern is neck extension worsening a spinal injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway positioning does not meaningfully raise ICP; the concern is spinal movement from neck extension.
distractorExplanations.d: The head-tilt/chin-lift is usually the more effective maneuver; it is avoided in trauma because of neck extension, not efficacy.

prompt: Wheezing is most commonly associated with:

options.text: Upper airway swelling at the larynx
Fluid in the alveoli of the lungs
Lower airway bronchoconstriction
Collapse of a lung from pneumothorax

explanation: Expiratory wheeze reflects narrowed lower airways; still assess for other causes. Asthma and COPD exacerbations are the classic causes.

distractorExplanations.a: Laryngeal swelling causes high-pitched inspiratory stridor, not the expiratory wheezing of narrowed bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales); wheezing comes from narrowed lower airways.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumothorax causes diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side, not wheezing.

prompt: A patient with inadequate breathing should receive

A nasopharyngeal airway with blow-by oxygen
Assisted positive-pressure ventilation (e.g., BVM)

explanation: Inadequate rate/depth needs assisted ventilation; oxygen alone does not ventilate.

distractorExplanations.a: A nonrebreather adds oxygen but does not move air; inadequate rate or depth requires assisted ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: CPAP needs an alert patient who breathes adequately on their own; inadequate breathing calls for BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: An NPA keeps the airway open but does not ventilate, and blow-by oxygen cannot correct poor ventilation.

prompt: CPAP in EMS (when indicated and available) primarily helps patients with:

options.text: Respiratory distress from conditions like CHF/pulmonary edema
Respiratory distress from a suspected tension pneumothorax
Inadequate breathing with a decreased level of responsiveness
Respiratory distress with systolic BP below 90 mm Hg

explanation: CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing cooperative patient; not for arrest or complete obstruction. It stents the airways open and improves oxygenation.

distractorExplanations.b: Positive pressure can enlarge a pneumothorax; suspected pneumothorax is a CPAP contraindication.
distractorExplanations.c: CPAP needs an alert patient who protects their airway and breathes adequately; this patient needs BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypotension is a CPAP contraindication because positive pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output.

prompt: Cyanosis indicates

options.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Significant hypoxemia
Severe anemia with normal SpO2
Peripheral vasodilation

explanation: Central cyanosis is a late, serious sign of poor oxygenation. It calls for urgent airway, oxygen, and ventilation assessment.

distractorExplanations.a: CO poisoning typically does not cause cyanosis; skin color and pulse oximetry can look falsely normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Anemia causes pallor; cyanosis needs enough deoxygenated hemoglobin, which anemic patients may lack.
distractorExplanations.d: Vasodilation causes flushed, red skin; the bluish color of cyanosis reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin.

prompt: A patient with severe asthma is wheezing less than before and becoming drowsy with poor air movement. This most likely indicates

options.text: The attack is resolving as the bronchospasm eases
Drowsiness as an expected side effect of nebulized albuterol
Worsening obstruction and impending respiratory failure
Hyperventilation from anxiety lowering CO2 levels

explanation: Silent chest/fatigue with drowsiness signals exhaustion and failure—support ventilation and ALS.

distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with drowsiness and poor air movement means too little airflow to wheeze — a silent chest, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: Albuterol causes tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety, not sedation; drowsiness here signals exhaustion.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation causes rapid breathing and tingling, not drowsiness with poor air movement.

prompt: The preferred method to open the airway of a trauma patient with possible c-spine injury is

options.text: Head-tilt/chin-lift once a rigid cervical collar is applied
Sniffing position with the head slightly extended back
Jaw-thrust after log-rolling the patient onto one side
Jaw-thrust while maintaining manual cervical stabilization

explanation: Jaw-thrust minimizes cervical movement in trauma airway opening.

distractorExplanations.a: A collar does not prevent the extension of a head-tilt; jaw-thrust with manual stabilization is used instead.
distractorExplanations.b: The sniffing position extends the neck; it is for non-trauma airway positioning, not suspected c-spine injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolling before manual stabilization moves the spine; the jaw-thrust is done with the head held inline in the position found.

prompt: Adequate adult ventilation rate with a BVM for a patient with a pulse (general guideline concept) is approximately

options.text: About 1 breath every 5–6 seconds (roughly 10–12/min)
As fast as possible until the SpO2 reaches 100%
About 1 breath every 10–12 seconds (roughly 5–6/min)
30 compressions to 2 breaths, as in adult CPR

explanation: Avoid hyperventilation; deliver breaths that produce chest rise at an appropriate rate. Each breath should be just enough to produce visible chest rise.

distractorExplanations.b: Rapid ventilation causes hyperventilation, gastric inflation, and reduced venous return; aim for 10–12 per minute.
distractorExplanations.c: Five to six breaths per minute under-ventilates an adult with a pulse; deliver one breath every 5–6 seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: 30:2 is the CPR ratio for a pulseless patient; a patient with a pulse receives rescue breaths without compressions.

prompt: Suctioning an adult patient's airway should be limited to approximately

options.text: No more than about 5 seconds per adult attempt
No more than about 15 seconds per attempt
No more than about 30 seconds per attempt
One attempt, then switch to finger sweeps

explanation: Brief suction clears the airway; prolonged suction worsens hypoxia—reoxygenate between attempts. Monitor oxygenation during and between attempts.

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is the infant limit; adults can be suctioned for up to about 15 seconds per attempt.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty seconds doubles the adult limit and causes hypoxia and vagal bradycardia.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeated brief suction passes with reoxygenation are acceptable; blind finger sweeps can push material deeper.

prompt: A nonrebreather mask is most appropriate when:

options.text: The patient is apneic and needs artificial ventilation
A COPD patient needs precise low-flow oxygen titration
A breathing patient needs high-concentration oxygen
A stable patient with SpO2 of 93% needs mild supplementation

explanation: NRB delivers high FiO2 to spontaneously breathing patients; apneic patients need BVM/advanced airway support. The patient must also be able to tolerate the mask.

distractorExplanations.a: Apnea requires positive-pressure ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: Precise FiO2 titration is the job of a Venturi mask; a nonrebreather delivers high, non-adjustable concentrations.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild hypoxemia in a stable patient is usually titrated with a nasal cannula toward 94%; the NRB is for high-concentration needs.

Give 2 rescue breaths and recheck the pulse for 1 minute
Give rescue breaths at 1 every 6 seconds without compressions
Check blood glucose before starting compressions

explanation: Cardiac arrest care prioritizes compressions and early defibrillation.

distractorExplanations.b: Compressions start immediately (C-A-B), and pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds in a suspected arrest.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient with a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.

prompt: High-quality adult CPR compression depth is approximately

options.text: About 1.5 inches (4 cm)
At least 2 inches (5 cm)
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)
One-half of the chest's depth

explanation: AHA-aligned adult depth is at least 2 inches with full recoil and adequate rate. Allow full chest recoil after each compression.

distractorExplanations.c: Depths beyond about 2.4 inches (6 cm) increase injury risk without benefit; the adult target is 2–2.4 inches.

prompt: An AED advises a shock. You should

options.text: Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds before shocking
Resume CPR for 2 minutes, then shock at the next analysis
Ensure no one is touching the patient, deliver the shock
Keep compressing while the AED delivers the shock

explanation: Clear, shock, then immediate CPR minimizes interruptions. Then immediately resume CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: A pulse check delays defibrillation; once the AED advises a shock, clear the patient and shock without a pulse check.
distractorExplanations.b: An advised shock is delivered now; delaying it lowers the chance of converting VF or pulseless VT.

prompt: Aspirin is given in suspected ACS (per protocol) primarily because it

options.text: Dissolves existing coronary clots like a fibrinolytic in the field
Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain
Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose
Inhibits platelet aggregation and may limit clot progression

explanation: Antiplatelet effect of aspirin is a key early ACS treatment when not contraindicated.

distractorExplanations.b: Coronary vasodilation is the action of nitroglycerin; aspirin is given as an antiplatelet agent.

prompt: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated when:

options.text: The patient has used a PDE-5 inhibitor recently or has hypotension
The patient has chest pain that started more than 12 hours ago
The patient's systolic blood pressure is 150 mm Hg with a headache
The patient already chewed 324 mg of aspirin for this episode

explanation: Nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension with PDE-5 drugs or low BP.

distractorExplanations.b: Symptom duration does not contraindicate nitroglycerin; contraindications are low BP and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic of 150 is above the hypotension cutoff (about 90–100 mm Hg); headache is a common side effect, not a contraindication.

Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness

prompt: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is suggested by:

A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 readings

A loose dressing with the patient in shock position

prompt: Evisceration management includes:

options.text: Gently replace the organs, then cover with moist dressing
Cover organs with moist sterile dressing and occlusive cover
Cover the organs with dry sterile gauze secured by a tight wrap
Give small sips of water to treat the developing shock

explanation: Keep organs moist and protected; replacement is a surgical task. Do not push the organs back inside.

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing eviscerated organs risks injury and contamination; reduction is a surgical task, so cover them in place.
distractorExplanations.c: Dry gauze adheres to and dries the bowel, and a tight wrap compresses the organs; use moist sterile plus occlusive.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal injury patients are kept NPO because they may need surgery and oral fluids risk vomiting and aspiration.

prompt: A patient with a penetrating chest wound develops worsening dyspnea and JVD. You should suspect

options.text: Simple pneumothorax without pressure buildup
Flail chest with a paradoxical segment
Tension pneumothorax physiology
Hemothorax causing hypovolemic shock

explanation: Penetrating chest trauma with distress/JVD raises tension pneumothorax concern—rapid transport/ALS. Support ABCs and request ALS per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: A simple pneumothorax causes dyspnea but not JVD; distended neck veins signal rising intrathoracic pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Flail chest results from blunt multiple rib fractures and does not explain JVD after a penetrating wound.
distractorExplanations.d: Massive hemothorax causes flat neck veins from blood loss, not distended neck veins.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1).

prompt: For an evisceration, appropriate EMT care includes:

options.text: Gently push the organs back in before dressing them
Cover with a dry sterile dressing secured by tape
Lay the patient flat with the legs straight to limit the pain
Cover with a moist sterile dressing and occlusive covering

explanation: Keep organs moist and protected; reduction is a surgical task. Do not push the organs back in.

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing eviscerated organs risks injury and contamination; reduction is a surgical task done in the hospital.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry dressings stick to and dry the organs, and adhesive should not touch them; use moist sterile plus occlusive.
distractorExplanations.c: Flexing the knees (if no spinal injury) relaxes the abdominal wall; straight legs increase tension on the wound.

prompt: A traction splint is generally indicated for:

options.text: Isolated midshaft femur fracture
Fracture of the pelvis with leg shortening
Fracture of the knee or lower leg
Hip dislocation with the leg rotated

explanation: Traction splints stabilize midshaft femurs when criteria are met; pelvis/spine need other care. Confirm there are no contraindications per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Pelvic fractures are a contraindication because the traction splint pushes against the pelvis.
distractorExplanations.c: Knee and lower-leg injuries are contraindications; traction is for midshaft femur fractures.
distractorExplanations.d: Hip injuries are a contraindication to traction splinting; the hip is splinted in the position found.

prompt: Cushing's triad (late increased ICP sign) includes:

options.text: Hypotension, tachycardia, and warm dry skin
Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations
Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds
Hypertension, tachycardia, and rapid, shallow respirations

explanation: Rising ICP can produce hypertension with reflex bradycardia and abnormal breathing.

distractorExplanations.a: That pattern fits shock more than Cushing.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade, not Cushing's triad.
distractorExplanations.d: Cushing's triad has reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia, along with irregular breathing.

prompt: When managing an amputation, you should:

options.text: Pack the part directly in ice so the tissue stays viable longer
Bag the part first, then dress the bleeding stump
Control bleeding, care for the stump, and transport the part
Submerge the part in sterile saline in a sealed container

explanation: Save the part properly for possible reimplantation while prioritizing life-threatening hemorrhage. Wrap the part cool and dry per protocol, not directly on ice.

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact freezes and damages the tissue; the bagged part is kept cool without touching ice.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong sequence: life-threatening bleeding at the stump is controlled first; the part is handled afterward.
distractorExplanations.d: Soaking waterlogs the tissue and hampers reattachment; the part is wrapped, not immersed.

prompt: SAMPLE history stands for:

options.text: Signs/Symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events
Signs/Symptoms, Assessment, Medications, Pertinent negatives, Last vitals, Events
Symptoms, Allergies, Mechanism, Pulse, Last meal, Exposure
Signs, Airway, Mental status, Pulse, Lungs, Extremities

explanation: SAMPLE structures medical history gathering.

distractorExplanations.b: Mixes in non-SAMPLE terms: A is Allergies, P is Past pertinent history, and L is Last oral intake.
distractorExplanations.c: Mechanism, pulse, and exposure belong to trauma assessment; in SAMPLE, M is Medications and P is Past history.
distractorExplanations.d: These are primary survey and physical exam elements, not the components of a SAMPLE history.

prompt: OPQRST is primarily used to assess

options.text: Past medical history and allergies
Pain/symptom characteristics
Level of responsiveness
Mechanism of injury details

explanation: OPQRST fleshes out the chief complaint symptom profile. The letters stand for Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, and Time.

distractorExplanations.a: Past history and allergies are gathered with the SAMPLE history, not OPQRST.
distractorExplanations.c: Responsiveness is assessed with AVPU or GCS, not with the OPQRST symptom profile.
distractorExplanations.d: Mechanism of injury is evaluated during scene size-up and trauma assessment, not by OPQRST.

prompt: A patient with stroke-like symptoms should be transported with priority on

options.text: Waiting on scene to see if symptoms resolve as in a TIA
Giving 324 mg of chewable aspirin before transport
Rapid transport to an appropriate stroke-capable facility
Transport to the nearest hospital even if it lacks stroke care

explanation: Time-sensitive stroke care needs rapid identification and transport; avoid delays and unsafe oral meds if swallow uncertain. Treatment depends on arrival within time windows.

distractorExplanations.a: A TIA cannot be distinguished from a stroke in the field; waiting loses the treatment window.
distractorExplanations.b: Aspirin is an ACS treatment; in stroke a hemorrhagic bleed cannot be excluded in the field and swallowing may be impaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Protocols direct stroke patients to stroke-capable centers when reachable in time, bypassing closer non-stroke hospitals.

prompt: Hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow may be treated with:

options.text: Insulin injection by EMT basic without protocol
Large IV potassium bolus
Withholding all sugar indefinitely
Oral glucose per protocol

explanation: Oral glucose is standard for symptomatic hypoglycemia when airway is protected.

distractorExplanations.a: EMT scope/protocols vary; insulin is not typical BLS.
distractorExplanations.b: Potassium is dangerous/inappropriate.
distractorExplanations.c: Sugar is the treatment.

prompt: Anaphylaxis treatment priority medication in EMS protocols is typically

options.text: Epinephrine
Oral antihistamine only as sole therapy
Aspirin
Nitroglycerin

explanation: IM epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis; antihistamines are adjuncts.

distractorExplanations.b: Antihistamines alone are insufficient for anaphylaxis.
distractorExplanations.c: Aspirin is ACS care.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitro is not anaphylaxis care.

prompt: Which best describes implied consent?

options.text: A bystander may give consent on behalf of an unresponsive adult
Unresponsive patients are treated as if they would want life-saving care
A competent adult agrees to treatment after hearing the risks and benefits
A parent agrees by phone to treatment of their injured minor child

explanation: Implied consent covers emergency care when a patient cannot decide; competent adults may refuse. This also covers patients impaired to the point they cannot decide.

distractorExplanations.a: Bystanders have no authority to consent; implied consent rests on the presumed wishes of the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes expressed (informed) consent, not implied consent.
distractorExplanations.d: A parent's agreement for a minor is expressed consent by a guardian; implied consent applies when no one can consent.

prompt: During extrication, the EMS provider's first responsibility is

options.text: Gaining access to the patient through the nearest open door
Starting a primary survey through the broken window
Scene safety and personal protective measures
Stabilizing the patient's cervical spine from the back seat

explanation: Rescuer safety enables sustained patient care; hazards must be controlled. These come before patient access.

distractorExplanations.a: Patient access comes after the vehicle is stabilized and hazards are controlled; rushing in endangers rescuers.
distractorExplanations.b: Patient contact comes after hazards are controlled and the vehicle is stabilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Entering before the vehicle is stabilized and hazards are controlled endangers the rescuer.

prompt: A DNR order is generally valid when:

options.text: A family member says the patient wouldn't want care
It was signed by the patient's attorney
The patient has a terminal illness diagnosis
It meets local legal requirements

explanation: Follow legal advance directives/DNR documentation; honor patient wishes when they request care and are competent. It must be presented and verified per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Verbal statements without valid documentation do not establish a DNR; begin care and contact medical direction.
distractorExplanations.b: A DNR order must be signed by a physician (and patient or proxy) per state law; an attorney's signature does not make it valid.
distractorExplanations.c: A terminal diagnosis alone does not create a DNR; a valid legal order is required.

prompt: Seizure management priorities include

options.text: Protect from injury, maintain airway, and time the seizure
Place a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
Hold the limbs firmly to stop the convulsions
Insert an OPA during the seizure to secure the airway

explanation: Protective positioning and airway support; never insert objects into the mouth. Do not force objects into the mouth.

distractorExplanations.b: Objects in the mouth can break teeth, cause airway obstruction, or injure the rescuer; nothing is placed between the teeth.
distractorExplanations.c: Restraining convulsing limbs does not stop the seizure and can cause fractures or soft-tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.d: A clenched jaw and active gag reflex make OPA insertion dangerous; use positioning, suction, or an NPA.

prompt: Which statement about ambulance emergency driving is correct?

options.text: Red signals may be passed at speed once sirens are on
Lights/sirens do not guarantee right-of-way
Seat belts are optional for providers in the back
Sirens give you right-of-way at intersections

explanation: Emergency privilege requires due regard; crashes during response harm everyone.

distractorExplanations.a: Most laws require slowing or stopping at red signals and proceeding with due regard for others.
distractorExplanations.c: Restraints protect providers.
distractorExplanations.d: Other drivers may not hear or yield; emergency vehicles request right-of-way rather than receive it.

prompt: Which patient is the highest triage priority in a multi-casualty incident (START concept)?

options.text: A walking wounded patient with a minor laceration
A patient with an isolated finger sprain who is ambulatory
An unresponsive patient with inadequate breathing after airway positioning attempts fail
A deceased patient with dependent lividity and obvious mortal injuries

explanation: Immediate (red) patients have life threats; expectant/dead and minor walking wounded are lower priority.

distractorExplanations.a: Walking wounded are delayed/minor.
distractorExplanations.b: Ambulatory minor injuries are low acuity.
distractorExplanations.d: Expectant/dead are not treated first in MCI triage.

prompt: Oral glucose is indicated for a diabetic patient who

options.text: Is hypoglycemic but too drowsy to follow commands
Has hyperglycemia with Kussmaul respirations
Is hypoglycemic and in the middle of an active seizure
Is hypoglycemic and can protect their airway/swallow

explanation: Oral sugar requires intact airway protective reflexes; unresponsive patients need other glucose routes/ALS.

distractorExplanations.a: Oral glucose requires a patient who can follow commands and swallow; a drowsy patient risks aspiration.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperglycemia needs different care.
distractorExplanations.c: A seizing patient cannot swallow safely; glucose must be given by another route through ALS.

prompt: A patient with suspected stroke within the window should be transported

options.text: Promptly to an appropriate stroke-capable facility
After a full neuro exam is completed on scene
To the closest hospital even without stroke services
After waiting several hours to see if symptoms resolve

explanation: Time-sensitive stroke care needs rapid transport and hospital alert. Prenotify the hospital when possible.

distractorExplanations.b: A detailed neuro exam can be done en route; delaying transport loses treatment time.
distractorExplanations.c: Protocols direct stroke patients to stroke-capable centers when reachable in time, bypassing closer hospitals.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting wastes the treatment window.

prompt: Which is a common early sign of compensated shock?

options.text: Hypotension with a weak, thready pulse and confusion
Tachycardia with cool, pale, diaphoretic skin
Bradycardia with warm, dry, flushed skin
Hypertension with bounding pulses and flushed skin

explanation: Compensation often raises HR and causes vasoconstriction signs before hypotension appears. Blood pressure is still near normal at this stage.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypotension with a thready pulse and confusion is decompensated (late) shock, not an early sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Bradycardia with warm, dry skin describes neurogenic shock, not early compensated hypovolemic shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertension is not a shock sign; compensation keeps BP near normal while heart rate rises.

prompt: When documenting a patient refusal, the EMT should:

options.text: Have a family member sign the refusal for the competent adult
Record only that the patient refused care, to limit your liability
Ensure the patient is informed of risks and document thoroughly
Transport under implied consent if the patient seems unwise

explanation: Informed refusal requires capacity, risk disclosure, and solid documentation. Confirm competence and involve medical direction per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: The competent patient signs their own refusal; family members may witness but cannot sign for them.
distractorExplanations.b: Brief notes increase liability; document risks explained, capacity, and the patient's understanding.
distractorExplanations.d: A competent adult may make an unwise choice; implied consent applies only to patients lacking capacity.
